name: The gateway rate limiter's counters are per-instance in-memory: N workers means N times the intended limit, and a restart resets every tenant's budget to full
symptom: Tenant rate limits drift upward under load and reset to nothing on deploys. A tenant configured for 60 requests/minute sustains several hundred per minute when the gateway has several workers, and every rolling restart hands every tenant a fresh full budget, so a tenant that has been correctly throttled all morning is throttlable again immediately after the next rollout. Because the limit is enforced per worker rather than globally, the error rate for a well-behaved tenant is not reproducible across gateway replicas.
root_cause: The middleware's own Limitations section lists it: 'Per-instance state (not shared across workers)', 'No cross-process state sharing', 'Memory growth with unique identifiers', 'State lost on instance restart', and the Overview explains why: 'Since WASM components are stateless, each worker thread maintains its own counter. For production, implement rate limiting at the router/host level with shared state.' The default example enforces 60 requests per minute per identifier, with identifier priority API Key then IP Address then Request ID — three different failure modes stacked on one scheme: an API-key identifier is per-worker-budgeted; an IP identifier fails outright behind NAT or a proxy (so all tenants behind one egress share one budget); and a Request ID identifier is per-request, so the 'limit' is meaningless because a client chooses it. 'Memory growth with unique identifiers' is the mirror problem: an identifier derived from anything high-cardinality grows gateway memory without bound.
workaround: Move the counter out of the guest module into shared state, which is what the docs prescribe, and enforce at the router or host level. Practically: put the limit in an external store (Redis or the platform's rate-limit service) keyed on a stable tenant identity derived from the API key, not IP and not a request id; make the gateway a single logical enforcer even with multiple replicas (an EPP active-active deployment shares no local state, so an in-memory counter there has the same defect). Choose the identifier deliberately: API key is the only one of the three defaults that identifies a tenant. If you cannot add shared state, treat the in-module limit as a coarse per-replica circuit breaker and size it at roughly limit/replicas — understanding that restarts restore full budget. Note the sibling auth example has the same shape: a single EXPECTED_API_KEY compiled into the guest module, which means rotation is a redeploy, not a config change.
notes: The generalisation: any rate limit enforced in a stateless or per-instance component is not a quota. This is not specific to WASM middleware — the same applies to any in-process limiter behind a load balancer with N replicas, where the effective global limit is N times the configured value. The honest state of the art for LLM serving is that per-tenant *compute* quotas are not solved at any layer (see ops-ratelimit-token-vs-request-count); what exists is per-tenant request rate, and it must be implemented in shared state to mean anything. SCHEME RECLASSIFIED (2026-10-04): was 'config'.
